title: Job 28:20–28
context: Job 28:20–28 concludes the hymn to wisdom, whose speaker is debated (Job, or the narrator in an interlude). The poem repeats its question about where wisdom comes from, says it is hidden from every living thing, and has Destruction and Death say they have only heard a rumor of it. The word rendered Destruction is Abaddon, a name linked with the realm of the dead. Then the answer comes: God understands its way and knows its place, because he sees the whole earth and set the wind, the waters, the rain, and the lightning in order. When he did so he saw wisdom and established it. To man he said, ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom. To depart from evil is understanding.’ In this verse the Hebrew word rendered “the Lord” is Adonai, not the divine name. The line echoes the narrator’s description of Job as one who feared God and turned away from evil (1:1) and the wisdom teaching of Proverbs (compare Proverbs 1:7, and 9:10, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.”). Both traditions treat 28:28 as shared ground about the source of wisdom.

verses.text: Where then does wisdom come from? Where is the place of understanding?
verses.arminianNotes: The poem asks again where wisdom comes from and where understanding has its place. Arminians see the repeated question as a refrain, which shapes the poem and marks the turn toward its answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the refrain as building suspense before the poem points to God. Both traditions read the question as the same one asked in verse 12, now asked once more after the search and the market have both failed.

verses.text: Seeing it is hidden from the eyes of all living, and kept close from the birds of the sky.
verses.arminianNotes: Wisdom is hidden from the eyes of all living and kept from the birds of the sky. Arminian readers see the poem echoing verse 7, where no bird of prey knew the miner’s path; wisdom is hidden even more deeply.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see wisdom’s hiddenness as pointing to its source beyond creation. Both traditions hold that wisdom is not discovered by any creature’s sight, but must be made known by God.

verses.text: Destruction and Death say, ‘We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.’
verses.arminianNotes: Destruction and Death say they have only heard a rumor of wisdom. Arminians see the realm of the dead personified, admitting that even it does not possess wisdom. The word rendered Destruction is Abaddon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as completing the survey: neither the living, the deep, the sea, nor the dead hold wisdom. Both traditions read Destruction and Death as poetic figures, not as persons the poem describes in detail.

verses.text: “God understands its way, and he knows its place.
verses.arminianNotes: God understands wisdom’s way and knows its place. Arminian readers see the turning point of the poem: what no creature can find, God knows, so wisdom must come from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God as the source and owner of wisdom. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and read the verse as the answer to the questions of verses 12 and 20.

verses.text: For he looks to the ends of the earth, and sees under the whole sky.
verses.arminianNotes: God looks to the ends of the earth and sees under the whole sky. Arminians see God’s complete knowledge of his creation, which contrasts with the limited reach of the miner’s eye in verse 10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sight as part of his sovereign wisdom over all things. Both traditions note that the LORD’s later speeches (chapters 38–41) develop this theme far more fully.

verses.text: He establishes the force of the wind. Yes, he measures out the waters by measure.
verses.arminianNotes: God establishes the force of the wind and measures out the waters. Arminian readers see God’s ordering of creation with precision, which shows that wisdom is woven into how he made the world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s governance of wind and water as an expression of his wisdom. Both traditions hold this as shared ground about God as Creator who orders creation by measure.

verses.text: When he made a decree for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunder,
verses.arminianNotes: God made a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning and thunder. Arminians see God setting boundaries and patterns for the weather, a picture of his wise rule over the forces people cannot control.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing God’s decree in creation. Both traditions read it as setting the scene for verse 27, where God sees and establishes wisdom at the time of creation.

verses.text: then he saw it, and declared it. He established it, yes, and searched it out.
verses.arminianNotes: Then God saw wisdom, declared it, established it, and searched it out. Arminian readers see wisdom linked to God’s work in creation, so that it belongs to him and is displayed in what he made.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and compare the picture of wisdom present at creation in Proverbs 8:22–31. Both traditions hold the details of how God relates to wisdom here with care, and agree that wisdom originates with God, not with any creature.

verses.text: To man he said, ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom. To depart from evil is understanding.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: God says to humans that the fear of the Lord is wisdom and departing from evil is understanding. Arminians see the poem’s answer: humans cannot find wisdom by searching, but they receive it by reverent trust and obedience. Here the Hebrew word rendered “the Lord” is Adonai.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the same truth in Proverbs 1:7, and in 9:10, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.” Both traditions hold this as shared ground, and note that the words echo the narrator’s description of Job as one who feared God and turned away from evil (1:1).
